## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Spring green-up sets the timing of fresh forage for the caribou and nesting geese of Wapusk National Park, on the western coast of Hudson Bay. However, whether green-up in the park has shifted in recent decades has not been established. To address this gap, this study aimed to estimate the trend in spring green-up between 2001 and 2024 and to test its association with snowmelt and spring temperature. Using Terra Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) surface reflectance, ERA5-Land reanalysis snow cover, and Environment and Climate Change Canada station temperature, the study estimated mid-green-up for 300 stratified pixels under an analysis plan fixed before any trend or relationship was examined. Mid-green-up averaged day of year (DOY) 180 and showed no detectable trend (Theil–Sen +0.03 days/yr, 95% CI −0.33 to +0.47), although the record can only reliably detect trends of about 0.7–0.9 days/yr. In contrast, later snow-off was associated with later green-up (5.4 days per standard deviation, R² = 0.52), and April–May thawing degree days accounted for a further 25% of the variance, for a combined R² of 0.77, although the contribution of warmth depended on how the temperature window was drawn. The findings of this study first demonstrate that the timing of fresh forage in Wapusk is better predicted by the conditions of a given spring than by the calendar. Secondly, a supplementary study found that a sandboxed coding agent improved the green-up method on held-out synthetic data but weakened its year-to-year fidelity on real pixels, which suggests that agents in research pipelines should be scored on the statistic the science depends on.

## Introduction

Wapusk National Park covers 11,475 km² of peatland, fen, coastal tundra, and open spruce forest south and east of Churchill, Manitoba, and its vegetation supports polar bears that summer on land as well as caribou and geese whose breeding success depends on the timing of high-quality forage. Doiron et al. [-@doiron2013] demonstrated on Bylot Island that the date on which NDVI reaches 50% of its annual maximum predicts the peak in plant nitrogen concentration, and Mallory et al. [-@mallory2020] reported that the start of green-up on the Qamanirjuaq caribou calving grounds, north-west of Hudson Bay, advanced by 7.25 days between 2004 and 2016. Whether a similar shift has occurred in Wapusk, however, has not been tested, and an earlier exploratory analysis in this repository produced trend estimates that changed between runs of identical code.

To bridge this gap, this research estimated spring mid-green-up for Wapusk from daily MODIS reflectance and tested its trend and its association with snowmelt and spring warmth. For this research, three alternative hypotheses were proposed:

1. **(H1)** Spring mid-green-up in Wapusk National Park advanced (occurred earlier) between 2001 and 2024.
2. **(H2)** In years with later snow-off, mid-green-up occurs later.
3. **(H3)** Spring thawing degree days explain variation in mid-green-up beyond that explained by snow-off.

The hypotheses, definitions, and models were committed in a pre-registration (`prereg.md`) before any trend or driver relationship was examined, and H1 was framed as an estimate with a confidence interval, interpreted against the smallest trend the record could detect.

## Methods

This section presents the methods used in this study. It begins with an overview of the study area and the pixel sample (*2.1*), and the subsequent subsections detail the data acquisition process (*2.2*), the estimation of mid-green-up (*2.3*), the predictors (*2.4*), and the statistical analysis (*2.5*). The peer-reviewed basis for every method, and the sensitivity test behind each parameter that the literature does not fix, are documented in `docs/methods_justification.md`.

### Area of Study

Wapusk National Park lies within the Hudson Bay Lowlands, in the transition between boreal forest and Arctic tundra (@fig-study-area). Per-pixel phenology was estimated on a fixed sample rather than on a park-wide mean, because a mean over whichever pixels happen to be cloud-free on a given day mixes landscapes with different timing. Candidate pixels were drawn at random from the 53,164 MODIS 500 m grid cells inside the park boundary; those with more than 10% surface water [@pekel2016] were excluded, and 75 pixels were retained in each of four ESA WorldCover [@zanaga2022] strata (forest, shrub and grass, wetland, and moss and lichen). Annual values were weighted by each stratum's share of dry land [@olofsson2014], so the results describe the drier ~70% of the park, which is 57% wetland, 33% shrub and grass, 7% moss and lichen, and 2% forest.

![Wapusk National Park and the 300 sample pixels, by land-cover stratum.](../results/figures/study_area.png){#fig-study-area width=50%}

### Data Acquisition

Data were acquired using the Google Earth Engine Python API [@gorelick2017] and the Meteorological Service of Canada GeoMet API for the period 2001–2024 (@tbl-data). All code is in the project repository, and every dataset is listed with its licence and citation in `DATA.md`.

### Mid-Green-Up

To calculate NDVI [@tucker1979] from the MODIS surface reflectance data, the image collection was first quality controlled using the cloud, shadow, snow, adjacency, and view-angle bits of the state and quality bands, and NDVI was then computed as the normalized difference of bands `sur_refl_b02` and `sur_refl_b01`. For each pixel, a dormant baseline was set at the 5th percentile of snow-free NDVI outside the growing season, following the pixel-specific winter NDVI of Beck et al. [-@beck2006] and the dormant-value rule of MCD12Q2 [@gray2019guide], and snow-flagged days before melt were anchored at that baseline. Each season was then smoothed with a Savitzky–Golay filter fitted to the upper envelope [@chen2004; @jonsson2004], and mid-green-up was taken as the first day on which the curve reached half of its seasonal amplitude above the baseline [@white1997], as shown in @fig-example-fits. This amplitude-based definition was used rather than the 50%-of-maximum rule of Doiron et al. [-@doiron2013], because in 92% of Wapusk pixels the snow-free dormant NDVI already exceeds half of the summer peak, so the maximum-based date cannot be defined once snow is masked. The annual value was the area-weighted median across valid pixels, of which there were between 227 and 300 in each year.

![Three randomly drawn pixel-years, showing snow-free observations, snow anchors at the baseline, the Savitzky–Golay fit, and the estimated mid-green-up.](../results/figures/example_fits.png){#fig-example-fits}

### Predictors

Snow-off was defined as the day after the last spring day on which park-mean ERA5-Land snow cover was at or above 50%. ERA5-Land was chosen over the Churchill station before any relationship with green-up was examined, because the station lacked a usable spring snow record in 9 of 24 years, and because ERA5-Land and MODIS snow-off [@hall2002] agreed closely (r = 0.81) despite their independent sources. As ERA5-Land overestimates snow-cover duration [@urraca2023], snow-off is used as an index of year-to-year variation rather than as an absolute melt date. Thawing degree days (TDD) were the sum of positive daily mean temperatures at the Churchill climate station between 1 April and 31 May, a window chosen to end before the earliest plausible green-up, as both snowmelt and spring temperature shape tundra phenology [@assmann2019; @bjorkman2015]; the spliced station record agrees closely with the homogenized Churchill series [@vincent2020].

### Analysis

The trend (H1) was estimated as a Theil–Sen slope [@sen1968] with Mann–Kendall tests [@hamed1998; @yue2002; @yuewang2002], and the smallest detectable trend was simulated before the response was examined [@weatherhead1998]. The association with snow-off (H2) was estimated with least squares on standardized predictors, and the contribution of TDD beyond snow-off (H3) with a nested F-test and bootstrap confidence intervals [@efron1993]. Because warm springs also melt snow early, the explained variance was partitioned with commonality analysis [@seibold1979; @raymukherjee2014] and read as a single chain from warmth through melt to green-up rather than as independent effects. All three hypotheses were re-estimated under 24 combinations of smoother, threshold, mask, and aggregation, and again under one-at-a-time changes to each parameter that the literature does not fix. The MCD12Q2 product served as a comparison, although because it derives from the same MODIS reflectance, agreement with it demonstrates consistency rather than accuracy.

## Results

Mid-green-up averaged DOY 180 (late June), with a standard deviation of 7.5 days, and ranged from DOY 165 in 2006 to DOY 196 in 2009 (@fig-series). The series agreed with MCD12Q2 (r = 0.90), although it ran 8.3 days later on average, an offset that showed no trend over time. @tbl-results summarises the three hypotheses.

![Annual mid-green-up from this study and from MCD12Q2, with the Theil–Sen trend of this study's series.](../results/figures/greenup_series.png){#fig-series}

| Hypothesis | Estimate | 95% CI | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| H1: green-up advanced | +0.03 days/yr | −0.33 to +0.47 | Not supported |
| H2: later snow-off, later green-up | +5.4 days per SD (R² = 0.52) | 3.1 to 7.7 | Supported |
| H3: TDD beyond snow-off | ΔR² = 0.25 (F-test p < 0.001) | 0.08 to 0.47 (BCa) | Supported, window-dependent |

: Results for the three pre-registered hypotheses. {#tbl-results}

### Trend (H1)

Mid-green-up showed no detectable trend between 2001 and 2024, as the Theil–Sen slope was +0.03 days/yr (95% CI −0.33 to +0.47) and all four Mann–Kendall variants gave p between 0.60 and 0.86. The pre-registered power analysis put the minimum detectable trend at about 0.9 days/yr, and across the 24 specifications the lower bound of the interval ranged from −0.33 to −0.72 days/yr (@fig-multiverse). Over the 2004–2016 window studied by Mallory et al. [-@mallory2020], the slope was −0.31 days/yr (CI −1.57 to +0.83), and onset at 15% of the amplitude trended at −0.27 to −0.61 days/yr across smoothers and masks.

![Theil–Sen slope and 95% CI under each of the 24 specifications; the pre-registered primary specification is shown in orange.](../results/figures/multiverse.png){#fig-multiverse}

### Snow-Off (H2)

Snow-off was associated with about half of the year-to-year variation, as each standard deviation (15 days) of later melt corresponded to green-up 5.4 days later (95% CI 3.1–7.7, R² = 0.52; @fig-drivers). The association held across all 24 specifications and under resampling of pixels, although it weakened to R² = 0.36 when the two most extreme years (2004 and 2009) were removed, and to R² = 0.27 (p = 0.05) when only the 15 years of genuine station snow-off were used.

![Mid-green-up against ERA5-Land snow-off and Churchill April–May thawing degree days.](../results/figures/drivers_scatter.png){#fig-drivers}

### Spring Warmth (H3)

TDD accounted for a further 25% of the variance (BCa 95% CI 8–47%), and together the two predictors explained 77% of it, with a leave-one-year-out error of 4.1 days against 7.6 days for the long-term mean. Of the explained variance, 43% was shared between the two predictors, 33% was unique to TDD, and 24% was unique to snow-off, although the bootstrap intervals for each share were wide. This contribution was the most sensitive result, as ending the window on 15 May rather than 31 May reduced it from 0.25 to 0.09 (p = 0.04).

## Discussion

The results do not support the acceptance of alternative hypothesis one (H1), as no advance in green-up was detectable, but they support the acceptance of alternative hypotheses two (H2) and three (H3). These findings suggest that green-up timing in the drier part of Wapusk varies far more from one spring to the next than it has changed over the 24-year record, as late melt and a cold spring in 2009 delayed it by about two weeks, while an early, warm spring in 2006 advanced it by a similar margin.

The absence of a trend is compatible with Mallory et al. [-@mallory2020], since the 2004–2016 slope falls within the range they reported, and it suggests that a decade of earlier springs did not persist across the longer record. This pattern resembles the long-term record from Zackenberg in north-east Greenland, where earlier advances in spring phenology have given way to little directional change [@schmidt2023]. Furthermore, Assmann et al. [-@assmann2019] found that phenology advanced only where snowmelt advanced, and that regional sea ice did not explain the variation, which points to local snowmelt rather than Hudson Bay sea ice as the more plausible control in Wapusk.

The strong shared component between snow-off and TDD is consistent with a single chain in which warm springs bring earlier melt and earlier green-up. This study cannot separate the effect of warmth before melt from its effect on the pace of growth after melt, however, because in four years the temperature window closed before snow-off, and because the contribution of warmth depended on where the window ended. In essence, the timing of fresh forage in Wapusk appears to be predictable from spring conditions in a given year, to within about four days, rather than from the calendar.

### Limitations

The main limitations of this research are five-fold. First, 24 years offer limited sensitivity to trends, and most specifications cannot exclude an advance of 0.56 days/yr. Second, the driver models rest on 24 points, and the snow-off association weakens without the two most extreme years or when only station data are used. Next, the predictors are coarse, as ERA5-Land resolves the park at about 9 km and the thawing degree days come from a single coastal station, and the contribution of warmth depends on the choice of window. Furthermore, the results describe the drier ~70% of the park, and the land-cover map used for weighting classifies wetland poorly [@worldcoverpvr2022]. Lastly, every comparison is between MODIS retrievals, so no ground phenology was available to validate the dates themselves.

## Future Work

Future studies could extend the record and increase its sensitivity to trends with Landsat and Sentinel-2 imagery, which would also cover the wetter margins of the park that the 500 m sample excludes. Ground phenology from the Churchill area, such as plot records from the Churchill Northern Studies Centre or the long-term goose research at La Pérouse Bay, would turn the comparison with MCD12Q2 into validation. Additionally, a principled temperature window, such as degree days counted from snow-off, could be pre-registered and tested, and the spatial pattern of trends and driver effects could be mapped from coast to inland. Lastly, these spring conditions could be tested as predictors of the timing of caribou and goose use of the park, which would connect the results to the management questions that motivated them.

## Conclusion

This study sought to establish whether green-up in Wapusk National Park has shifted since 2001 and how its timing relates to snowmelt and spring warmth. No trend was detectable under any of 24 processing specifications, although the record cannot exclude moderate advances, and snow-off and spring warmth together accounted for 77% of the year-to-year variation. Overall, these results suggest that monitoring the timing of forage in Wapusk should focus on spring snowmelt and temperature in a given year rather than on long-term trends, and that a longer and finer record will be needed to detect the moderate advances reported elsewhere in the region.

## Supplementary Study: A Sandboxed Agent Loop {.unnumbered}

This study also examined what happens when a coding agent is given one narrow part of a research pipeline to improve. Following the pattern of a single editable program judged by a fixed external evaluator [@karpathy2026; @novikov2025], with held-out grading and rule-breaking checks as in MLE-bench [@chan2024], a Claude Code agent could edit only the green-up method, while a driver outside its control scored each change on 1,800 synthetic seasons and kept it only if the error fell. After 33 iterations, the frozen candidate was scored once on held-out synthetic data and on real pixels, and it was kept off the confirmatory analysis throughout.

The agent kept 8 changes and never attempted an edit outside its file, and its final version cut held-out synthetic error from 4.65 to 4.39 days (@fig-agent). On real pixels, however, it lowered the park-wide annual agreement with MCD12Q2 from 0.900 to 0.881, so it did not qualify for the analysis. An ablation located the trade-off: an early change (iteration 8) improved held-out error without losing year-to-year fidelity, whereas a later change (iteration 16) bought lower pixel bias at the cost of that fidelity, and a keep-if-better rule could not see the difference. Four of the eight kept changes only removed lines to reduce a line-count penalty, which the agent described openly, and on held-out seasons built from real NDVI shapes every method erred by more than 8 days, against 2–4 days on synthetic seasons.

These results suggest three lessons for agents in research. First, a single score is gamed even by an agent that reports its changes honestly, so evaluators should reject changes that leave outputs unchanged. Next, per-season accuracy diverged from the statistic the science depends on, so the evaluator should score that statistic directly and keep every version that is not dominated across objectives. Lastly, keeping the agent off the inference path meant that none of its changes could move the reported result, and none did; the full account is in `autoresearch/LESSONS.md`.

![Left: score on the visible synthetic benchmark by iteration. Right: held-out synthetic error against annual agreement with MCD12Q2 for each kept version (blue) and for the frozen candidate with one change removed (green).](../results/figures/autoresearch_dynamics.png){#fig-agent}

## Data & Software {.unnumbered}

All code, derived data, figures, the pre-registration, and an AI referee report are available at <https://github.com/anniebritton/ISAMR-Research>, and an interactive version of these results is available at <https://anniebritton.github.io/ISAMR-Research/>. The pipeline is written in Python and uses the Earth Engine API, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, and pyMannKendall. The pre-registration was committed at 23:12:06 UTC on 14 October 2026, after data extraction and four seconds before the confirmatory run, and analyses added afterwards are listed under Deviations in `prereg.md`. The analysis code, pre-registration, and first draft were produced by an AI coding agent (Claude Code) under the author's direction, and the author is responsible for the research questions, design decisions, and conclusions.
